area: Area IV. Takeoffs, Landings, and Go-Arounds
objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain how ground effect and weight transfer get an airplane off a soft field, and fly a soft-field takeoff and climb to ACS standards, including what to do if the takeoff goes wrong.
why: Grass, mud, sand and snow fight your acceleration and can keep a normal takeoff from ever reaching flying speed [[24:145|AFH 6-13]]. About 20 percent of yearly GA accidents happen in takeoff and departure climb [[24:133|AFH 6-1]].

prereading.what: Ground effect on takeoff, Vx and Vy, soft/rough-field takeoff, common errors, rejected takeoff/engine failure, noise abatement.
prereading.label: AFH Ch 6, 6-10 to 6-14

prereading.what: Ground effect: what it does to airflow, induced drag and instruments.
prereading.label: PHAK Ch 5, 5-11 to 5-12

prereading.what: Left-turning tendencies: torque, corkscrew slipstream, gyroscopic action, P-factor.
prereading.label: PHAK Ch 5, 5-30 to 5-33

prereading.what: Runway surface, wind, weight and density altitude effects on takeoff distance.
prereading.label: PHAK Ch 11, 11-12 to 11-16

warmup: On a grass strip after a rain, your wheels sink a little into the turf. If you hold the nose down like a normal takeoff, what do you think happens to your acceleration? What could you do with the elevator to help?

key_terms.def: A takeoff surface like tall grass, soft sand, mud or snow that adds drag and slows acceleration [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].
Moving the airplane's weight from the wheels to the wings as early as possible by holding a nose-high attitude [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].
Better performance very close to the ground, normally up to about one wingspan high, because the ground reduces wingtip vortices and induced drag [[24:142|AFH 6-10]].
Drag that comes from making lift; it is biggest at low speed and high angle of attack [[1:108|PHAK 5-11]].
Best angle of climb speed: most altitude for a given distance over the ground [[24:142|AFH 6-10]].
Best rate of climb speed: most altitude in a given time [[24:142|AFH 6-10]].
At high angle of attack the down-moving propeller blade takes a bigger bite, yawing the nose left [[1:129|PHAK 5-32]].
Slow flight where a lower airspeed needs more power to hold altitude [[1:267|PHAK 11-11]]; climbing out of ground effect too slowly can put you there [[1:268|PHAK 11-12]].
Stopping a takeoff while still on the runway because something is wrong [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].

chunks.title: Why soft fields need a different takeoff

body.p: Tall grass, soft sand, mud and snow drag on the wheels. They cut acceleration and may keep you from ever reaching takeoff speed with a normal technique [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].

Performance charts assume a paved, level, smooth, dry runway. Any surface that is not hard and smooth makes the ground roll longer, because tires sink into soft, grassy or muddy ground [[1:268|PHAK 11-12]].
The fix: get the weight off the wheels and onto the wings as fast as you can [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].

bullets: Hold a relatively high angle of attack (nose-high) as early as possible in the roll [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].
Lower the flaps before the takeoff if the manufacturer recommends it. Flaps give extra lift and move weight to the wings sooner [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].
Keep rolling. Don't stop while lining up; stopping on mud or snow can bog the airplane down [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].
The same technique helps on a rough field: get off quickly to avoid damaging the landing gear [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].

callout.text: A soft-field takeoff is not a short-field takeoff. Short-field rolls on all the weight to VX; soft-field lifts the nose early and lifts off below a safe climb speed [[24:145|AFH 6-13]] [[24:143|AFH 6-11]].
Exact flap setting and speeds for your airplane come from the POH/AFM. If the AFH and the POH differ, the POH wins [[24:133|AFH 6-1]].

check.q: Why do you hold the nose high during a soft-field takeoff roll?
check.a: To transfer weight from the wheels to the wings as fast as possible, which cuts the drag of the soft surface [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].

chunks.title: Ground effect: the cushion you take off in

body.p: Close to the ground, the surface squeezes the airflow around the wing. Upwash, downwash and wingtip vortices get smaller, so induced drag drops [[1:108|PHAK 5-11]]. It normally works up to a height of about one wingspan [[24:142|AFH 6-10]].
The effect grows fast as you get lower:
Numbers from [[1:108|PHAK 5-11]]. The AFH rounds them to about 25 and 50 percent [[24:142|AFH 6-10]].
Because drag is lower, the airplane can fly at a lower indicated airspeed than normal while in ground effect [[1:108|PHAK 5-11]]. That is the trick a soft-field takeoff uses.
As you climb OUT of ground effect, the airplane [[24:142|AFH 6-10]]:

bullets: Needs more angle of attack to make the same lift.
Gets more induced drag and needs more thrust.
Pitches up (more downwash on the tail), so it needs less elevator.
Shows a higher indicated airspeed, because static pressure drops.

body.p: In ground effect, extra static pressure makes the airspeed indicator and altimeter read a bit low, and the VSI often shows a descent [[24:142|AFH 6-10]].

callout.text: Ground effect can let you lift off but not climb. At high density altitude, high temperature or max gross weight, the airplane may fly in ground effect but be unable to climb out of it and clear obstacles [[24:143|AFH 6-11]].
Leaving ground effect: "More AOA, more drag, nose up, airspeed up."

check.q: Your wing is 1/10 of its span above the runway. About how much is induced drag reduced?
check.a: About 47.6 percent (AFH rounds to about 50 percent) [[1:108|PHAK 5-11]] [[24:142|AFH 6-10]].

chunks.title: VX and VY: which climb speed when

head: Speed
What it gives you
Use it for
rows: Most altitude per distance over the ground [[24:142|AFH 6-10]]
Most altitude per unit of time [[24:142|AFH 6-10]]
Normal climb once clear of obstacles [[24:145|AFH 6-13]]

body.p: VX is usually a little slower than VY. Your airplane's exact speeds are in the AFM/POH [[24:142|AFH 6-10]].
In some airplanes, being just 5 knots off the recommended speed can cut climb performance a lot. Fly the speed precisely [[24:142|AFH 6-10]].
Soft-field rule: stay in ground effect until at least VX. If there's an obstacle, climb at VX until it's cleared, then lower the nose to VY [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].

check.q: There are trees at the end of the grass strip. Which speed do you climb at first, and when do you change?
check.a: Climb at VX until the trees are cleared, then pitch for VY and clean up [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].

body.p: Check the POH/AFM performance charts before you go and decide if the takeoff and climb are safe for the conditions [[24:133|AFH 6-1]].

head: Factor
Effect on takeoff
rows: At least 21 percent more takeoff distance [[1:271|PHAK 11-15]]
Higher true airspeed needed, less thrust and acceleration [[1:272|PHAK 11-16]]
Soft, grassy, muddy or snowy surface

body.p: Take off as nearly into the wind as you can. A headwind gives you airspeed before you even move and lowers the groundspeed needed to fly [[24:135|AFH 6-3]].

callout.text: Tailwind takeoff? First check the POH/AFM says the airplane is approved for it and that you have enough performance and runway [[24:135|AFH 6-3]]. On a soft field, a tailwind stacks on top of the surface drag.

body.p: The worst takeoffs come from a mix of high gross weight, altitude, temperature and unfavorable wind [[1:272|PHAK 11-16]]. Pressure altitude and temperature, gross weight, wind, and runway slope and condition all go into your POH takeoff distance [[1:272|PHAK 11-16]].

check.q: A tailwind is 10 percent of your takeoff airspeed. About how much longer is your takeoff distance?

chunks.title: Left-turning tendencies in a nose-high roll

body.p: "Torque" (the left-turning tendency) has four parts [[1:127|PHAK 5-30]] [[1:128|PHAK 5-31]]:

bullets: Torque reaction: the engine turns the prop one way, the airplane wants to roll the other. On the ground it loads the left main wheel, adding friction and a pull to the left. Ground surface condition changes how strong this is [[1:128|PHAK 5-31]].
Corkscrew slipstream: strongest at high prop speed and low forward speed, like a takeoff. It hits the tail and yaws the nose [[1:128|PHAK 5-31]].
Gyroscopic action: any pitch change makes a yaw, and any yaw makes a pitch [[1:129|PHAK 5-32]].
P-factor: at high angle of attack, the down-moving blade bites more and pulls the nose left [[1:129|PHAK 5-32]].

body.p: A soft-field takeoff is full power, low speed and nose-high. That is exactly when the corkscrew slipstream and P-factor are strong [[1:128|PHAK 5-31]] [[1:129|PHAK 5-32]]. Expect the nose to go left and hold right rudder to keep straight [[24:135|AFH 6-3]].

callout.text: Add power smoothly. Abrupt power can yaw the airplane sharply left [[24:135|AFH 6-3]]. Steer with rudder, not brakes [[24:135|AFH 6-3]].

check.q: Why is P-factor strong during a soft-field takeoff roll?
check.a: You hold a high angle of attack at full power, so the down-moving blade takes a bigger bite and yaws the nose left [[1:129|PHAK 5-32]].

bullets: 1. Before the runway: finish the run-up and pre-takeoff checklists before taxiing onto the runway [[24:133|AFH 6-1]]. Set flaps as the POH recommends [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].
2. Radio and wind: announce on the CTAF, or get a takeoff clearance at a towered airport [[24:133|AFH 6-1]]. Check the windsock or other indicators [[24:138|AFH 6-6]].
3. Clear and verify: scan the approach and takeoff paths for traffic [[24:133|AFH 6-1]]. Check the heading indicator matches the runway number [[1:366|PHAK 14-32]].
4. Roll onto the runway without stopping, with crosswind controls in, and line up on centerline [[24:145|AFH 6-13]] [[24:138|AFH 6-6]].
5. Apply takeoff power smoothly and as fast as the engine accepts it. Check engine instruments [[24:145|AFH 6-13]] [[24:135|AFH 6-3]].
6. Add back-elevator pressure to raise the nose-wheel and hold a nose-high attitude. The wings take the weight [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].
7. Hold that attitude. The airplane flies itself off at a speed lower than a safe climb speed, thanks to ground effect [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].
8. Gently lower the nose with the wheels just clear of the surface. Stay in ground effect and accelerate to at least VX [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].
9. Climb at VX if there's an obstacle, otherwise at VY. Expect the nose to pitch up as you leave ground effect [[24:145|AFH 6-13]] [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].
10. After a positive rate of climb and at VY, retract gear and flaps (if equipped). After wet snow or slush, leave the gear down a bit to air-dry it [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].
11. Keep takeoff power to at least 500 feet above terrain or obstacles, then set climb power and trim [[24:137|AFH 6-5]].
12. Track the extended centerline with a crab for drift, and follow any noise abatement procedure [[24:140|AFH 6-8]] [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].

head: ACS standard
Tolerance
rows: Pitch attitude that moves weight from wheels to wings as rapidly as possible (ACS PA.IV.C.S8)
Lowest possible airspeed, stay in ground effect while accelerating to VX or VY (ACS PA.IV.C.S9)
VX or VY, +10/-5 knots during the climb (ACS PA.IV.C.S10)
After positive rate of climb verified, or per manufacturer (ACS PA.IV.C.S11)
Directional control and wind-drift correction throughout (ACS PA.IV.C.S13)

callout.text: Roll, raise, float, fly: keep Rolling, Raise the nose, Float in ground effect, then Fly away at VX/VY.

check.q: After lift-off, what do you do with the nose and why?
check.a: Lower it gently and stay in ground effect until at least VX; climbing out early can make the airplane settle back, even at full power [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].

body.p: From the AFH soft/rough-field list [[24:145|AFH 6-13]] [[24:146|AFH 6-14]]:

bullets: Not reviewing the AFM/POH and performance charts first.
Not clearing the area.
Too little back-elevator pressure early in the roll, so the angle of attack is too low.
Not cross-checking engine instruments after adding power.
Poor directional control.
Climbing too high after lift-off instead of leveling low in ground effect.
Abrupt or too much elevator when leveling off to accelerate.
Letting the airplane "mush" or settle back onto the surface.
Climbing out of ground effect before reaching climb speed.
Not expecting the pitch-up as the airplane leaves ground effect.

body.p: Why climbing out too slow is so bad: you can end up in the region of reversed command at a very low altitude. Even with full power, the airplane may not climb or even hold altitude. The only fix is to lower the nose to gain speed, which costs altitude [[1:268|PHAK 11-12]].

callout.text: Don't force it. Too much back-elevator before flying speed can give an excessive angle of attack, settling back to the runway, or even a stall [[24:137|AFH 6-5]].

check.q: Just after lift-off the airplane starts to sink back toward the grass. What likely went wrong?
check.a: You likely let it mush or tried to climb out of ground effect before reaching climb speed [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].

chunks.title: Risk: runway choice, wind, windshear and wake

body.p: Pick the runway using your skill, the airplane's performance, the distance you have and the wind. Run the POH numbers no matter how long the runway is [[1:272|PHAK 11-16]]. Check the Chart Supplement for surface type and slope [[1:268|PHAK 11-12]] [[1:269|PHAK 11-13]].

head: Hazard
What it does
What a good pilot does
rows: Upwind wing wants to rise; side-skipping can damage the gear [[24:139|AFH 6-7]]
Full aileron into the wind at the start, ease off as speed builds, rudder to stay straight, crab after lift-off [[24:138|AFH 6-6]] [[24:140|AFH 6-8]]
Headwind turning to tailwind drops airspeed and performance [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]]. On the runway the only sign may be slow airspeed buildup, masked by gusts [[28:270|AWH 22-15]]

Watch for frontal systems, thunderstorms, inversions and strong upper winds over 25 knots; be ready to react at once [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]]; listen for ATC and ATIS wind shear/microburst alerts [[28:400|AWH 26-33]]
About 21 percent longer takeoff for a tailwind of 10% of takeoff speed [[1:271|PHAK 11-15]]
Only if POH approves it and numbers work [[24:135|AFH 6-3]]
Vortices sink, then drift sideways 2-3 knots near the ground [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]]
Rotate before the larger airplane's rotation point and climb above its path; after its low approach or touch-and-go, wait at least 2 minutes [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]]
Longer roll, may never reach takeoff speed [[24:145|AFH 6-13]]
Use soft-field technique and POH data; get the weight on the wings early [[24:145|AFH 6-13]]

body.p: At low lift-off speeds the controls are less responsive and need more movement [[24:137|AFH 6-5]], so a soft-field lift-off leaves less control margin in gusts. In strong, gusty wind, the AFH advises an extra margin of speed before leaving the ground [[24:137|AFH 6-5]].

Finding the wind: ATC gives it at a towered field; otherwise get it from FSS or on the CTAF, and still check the wind indicators (windsock, tee, tetrahedron) because CTAF information may not be accurate [[1:354|PHAK 14-20]]. With no indicator at all, smoke drift shows wind direction, and flags, leaves and trees hint at speed [[34:227|AIM TBL 10-2-3]].

callout.text: A soft-field takeoff keeps you low and slow in ground effect for a while. Ask: can I stay above a big airplane's wake path, and will a gust or shear leave me any margin? If not, wait or pick another runway.

check.q: A larger airplane just did a touch-and-go on your runway in a light quartering wind. What does the AIM recommend?
check.a: Wait at least 2 minutes before your takeoff, since vortices can settle and drift along the runway [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]].

chunks.title: Risk: rejected takeoff, engine failure, and staying ahead

body.p: Rejected takeoff: before you roll, pick a point on the runway where you should be airborne. Not airborne there? Stop at once [[24:146|AFH 6-14]]. POH takeoff plus landing ground rolls give a good estimate of the runway you need to go and then stop [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].

bullets: Reasons to reject: bad engine, poor acceleration, runway incursion, traffic conflict [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].
How: power to idle, maximum braking while keeping directional control; fire means mixture to idle cutoff and mags off; always follow the POH emergency procedure [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].
On a soft field the surface itself slows you; on landing rolls, hard braking there can make the nose-wheel dig in [[24:195|AFH 9-24]]. Know your POH guidance.

body.p: Engine failure after lift-off: you have only seconds. In a climb attitude with no power you are at or near a stall. Lower the nose right away, use rudder to stay coordinated, and glide to a landing area, preferably straight ahead. Don't turn back unless trained for it and high enough [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].

Low-altitude stall/spin: many stall/spin accidents happen in takeoff and climb-out; premature flap retraction is one cause [[13:11|AC 61-67C 104b]]. Forcing the airplane up too early can stall it [[24:137|AFH 6-5]]. Raise flaps only after a positive climb [[1:109|PHAK 5-12]].
CFIT: high density altitude is a CFIT factor [[30:22|RMH 3-4]]. An airplane that can't climb out of ground effect may not clear obstacles [[24:143|AFH 6-11]].

Collisions: clear the approach and takeoff paths before taking the runway [[24:133|AFH 6-1]] and keep scanning in the climb [[24:138|AFH 6-6]]. Monitor CTAF from startup through taxi and departure [[17:13|AC 90-66C 10.4.2]].

Distractions: a small issue, like a gauge that reads wrong, can pull attention off flying the airplane [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]]. Until obstacles are cleared, keep your eyes outside, not on gear or flap handles [[24:144|AFH 6-12]]. Use a sterile flight deck from departure until clear of local airspace [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]].

callout.text: Engine quits on climb-out: NOSE DOWN, feet coordinated, land ahead.

check.q: Your engine quits at 200 feet just after a soft-field departure. What is your first action?
check.a: Lower the nose immediately to avoid a stall, keep it coordinated, and glide to a landing area mostly straight ahead [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].

scenario.title: Wet grass, warm afternoon, trees at the end
scenario.setup: You and a friend are at a small grass strip after morning rain. It's a hot afternoon, you're near max gross weight, and there's a line of trees past the far end. The windsock shows a light wind from behind you on the runway you taxied to. Your friend is chatting about lunch plans as you line up, and a radio call says a twin is on a 3-mile final for the other end.

questions.q: What do the wet grass, heat and weight do to your takeoff?
questions.a: All three lengthen the roll: soft grass adds drag, high density altitude cuts thrust, and more weight means a longer distance [[1:268|PHAK 11-12]] [[1:272|PHAK 11-16]] [[1:271|PHAK 11-15]]. Run the POH numbers first [[24:133|AFH 6-1]].

questions.q: Should you take off with that tailwind?
questions.a: Only if the POH approves it and performance works. A tailwind of 10% of takeoff speed adds about 21 percent to the distance [[24:135|AFH 6-3]] [[1:271|PHAK 11-15]]. Better: use the into-wind runway, after the twin lands.

questions.q: The twin lands. What about the trees and the hot day?
questions.a: Use the into-wind runway, pick an abort point, stay in ground effect to VX, then climb at VX until clear of the trees [[24:146|AFH 6-14]] [[24:145|AFH 6-13]]. Remember a hot, heavy airplane may lift off but not climb out of ground effect [[24:143|AFH 6-11]].

questions.q: You reach your abort point still on the ground. Now what?
questions.a: Reject the takeoff: power to idle, stop while keeping directional control, follow the POH [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].

questions.q: How do you handle your chatty friend?
questions.a: Brief a sterile flight deck from departure until clear of local airspace [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]]; distractions pull your attention from flying [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]].

skills.do: Complete the run-up and before-takeoff checklists before taxiing onto the runway.
skills.practice: Read and do each item aloud; finish everything while stopped on firm ground, not on the runway [[24:133|AFH 6-1]].

skills.do: Make the right radio calls (CTAF announcement or tower takeoff clearance).
skills.practice: Script your departure calls; monitor CTAF from startup through departure [[17:13|AC 90-66C 10.4.2]].

skills.do: Verify you are on the correct runway.
skills.practice: Set the heading bug to the runway heading and check heading vs runway before adding power [[1:366|PHAK 14-32]].

skills.do: Tell the examiner the wind direction, with or without a windsock.
skills.practice: Point out the windsock or segmented circle [[1:354|PHAK 14-20]]; with none, use smoke, flags or trees [[34:227|AIM TBL 10-2-3]].
Full aileron into a crosswind at the start of the roll, easing off as speed builds [[24:138|AFH 6-6]] [[24:139|AFH 6-7]].

skills.do: Clear the area, taxi onto the runway and align on centerline without stopping, while smoothly adding takeoff power.
skills.practice: Keep rolling with enough power; elevator back to unload the nose-wheel [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].

skills.do: Confirm takeoff power and normal engine and flight instrument indications.
skills.practice: Glance at RPM/oil pressure/airspeed alive early in the roll, then eyes outside [[24:135|AFH 6-3]].

skills.do: Hold a pitch attitude that moves weight to the wings as rapidly as possible.
skills.practice: Have your CFI show the nose-high attitude against the horizon; practice holding it [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].

skills.do: Lift off at the lowest possible airspeed and stay in ground effect while accelerating to VX or VY.
skills.practice: Practice the level-off just above the runway on a long runway first [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].

skills.do: Pitch for VX or VY and hold it +10/-5 knots during the climb (ACS PA.IV.C.S10).
skills.practice: Set attitude on the horizon, then check airspeed; don't chase the needle [[24:137|AFH 6-5]].

skills.do: Configure the airplane after a positive rate of climb (or per the manufacturer).
skills.practice: Say 'positive rate' before touching gear or flaps [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].

skills.do: Hold VX or VY +10/-5 knots to a safe maneuvering altitude (ACS PA.IV.C.S12).
skills.practice: Keep takeoff power to at least 500 feet above terrain or obstacles, then trim [[24:137|AFH 6-5]].

skills.do: Keep directional control and wind-drift correction through takeoff and climb.
skills.practice: Right rudder for left-turning tendencies; crab to track the extended centerline [[24:135|AFH 6-3]] [[24:140|AFH 6-8]].

skills.do: Follow noise abatement procedures if the airport has them.
skills.practice: Look them up in the Chart Supplement or ask the tower [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].

quiz.q: What is the main goal of the soft-field takeoff technique?
options: Transfer weight from the wheels to the wings as rapidly as possible
Roll with full weight on the wheels to VX
Keep the nose-wheel on the ground until VY
Use brakes to hold the airplane until full power
quiz.why: Holding a nose-high attitude early moves weight to the wings and cuts surface drag [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].

quiz.q: Ground effect normally occurs up to a height of about:
options: One-tenth of the wingspan
One wingspan
One-half of the wingspan
Two wingspans
quiz.why: Ground effect normally occurs up to an altitude equal to one wingspan [[24:142|AFH 6-10]].

quiz.q: With the wing at a height of one-fourth its span, induced drag is reduced by about:
options: 1.4 percent
47.6 percent
23.5 percent
75 percent
quiz.why: PHAK gives 23.5 percent at one-fourth span (AFH rounds to about 25 percent) [[1:108|PHAK 5-11]].

quiz.q: Right after a soft-field lift-off, you should:
options: Climb steeply at once to clear the surface
Gently lower the nose and stay in ground effect until at least VX
Retract the flaps to reduce drag
Reduce power to climb power
quiz.why: The airplane tends to settle as it leaves ground effect, so stay in it until at least VX [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].

quiz.q: As the airplane climbs out of ground effect, the airspeed indicator will:
options: Stay the same
Read lower
Read higher
Show zero
quiz.why: Static source pressure drops, so indicated airspeed increases [[24:142|AFH 6-10]].

quiz.q: There is an obstacle at the end of the field. After lift-off and accelerating in ground effect, you climb at:
options: VY until clear, then VX
VX until clear, then VY
Cruise climb speed
The lift-off speed
quiz.why: Climb at VX until the obstacle is cleared, then pitch for VY [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].

quiz.q: A tailwind equal to 10 percent of the takeoff airspeed increases takeoff distance by about:
options: 21 percent
19 percent
10 percent
50 percent
quiz.why: About 21 percent longer (a 10 percent headwind cuts it about 19 percent) [[1:271|PHAK 11-15]].

quiz.q: The engine fails during the initial climb. Your first action is to:
options: Turn back to the runway
Raise the flaps
Try a restart
Lower the nose to prevent a stall
quiz.why: At climb attitude with no power you are near a stall; lower the nose at once, then glide mostly straight ahead [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].

takeaways: Keep rolling and get the weight on the wings early with a nose-high attitude.
Lift off as slow as possible, then lower the nose and stay in ground effect to at least VX.
Leaving ground effect means more drag and a pitch-up; climbing out too slow can leave you unable to climb.
VX to clear obstacles, then VY, held +10/-5 knots (ACS PA.IV.C.S10).
Soft surface, heat, weight and tailwind all stack up; run the POH numbers and pick an abort point.
Engine quits on climb-out: nose down, land mostly straight ahead.
cfi_notes: Demo the nose-high roll attitude and the level-off height on a long paved runway before going to grass.
Students often climb out of ground effect too early or pull too hard at lift-off; examiners watch for the settle-back [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].
Point out the pitch-up as the airplane leaves ground effect; untrimmed students balloon [[24:142|AFH 6-10]].
Expect left yaw: full power, nose-high and slow is peak P-factor and slipstream effect. Coach right rudder [[1:129|PHAK 5-32]].
Have the student state the abort point and the engine-failure plan aloud before every takeoff [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].
Tailwheel version of this takeoff: AFH 14-4 (tail kept very low, elevator full up while taxiing on soft ground) [[24:290|AFH 14-4]].
Examiners may ask the ground effect induced-drag numbers and the four things that happen when leaving ground effect.
gaps: Airplane-specific numbers (flap setting, lift-off speed, VX/VY, soft-field distance corrections) come from the POH/AFM, not these sources.
No source here gives a specific procedure for rejecting a takeoff on a soft surface; AFH 6-14 is general and AFH 9-24 covers soft-field braking only for landing.

AC 00-54 (Pilot Windshear Guide), cited by the PHAK, was cancelled by the FAA in 2022; this lesson uses the Aviation Weather Handbook (FAA-H-8083-28B) instead. AWH 22-10 to 22-18 covers microburst effects, warning signs and the general principle of holding pitch attitude and accepting lower airspeed, but its encounter studies appear to involve large, crew-flown airplanes (crew coordination, stick shakers, aft body contact) and it gives no step-by-step windshear escape procedure for small airplanes. Get the airplane-specific technique from the POH/AFM and your CFI.
Local noise abatement procedures are airport-specific (Chart Supplement, local publications).

activities.title: In ground effect, or leaving it?
activities.intro: Tap a clue, then tap where it belongs.

items.t: Airspeed indicator and altimeter read a bit low
The VSI often shows a descent
The airplane can fly at a lower indicated airspeed
Needs more angle of attack for the same lift
More induced drag, so more thrust is needed
The nose tends to pitch up
Indicated airspeed goes up as static pressure drops

activities.title: What does it do to your takeoff?
activities.intro: Tap a condition, then its effect on the takeoff.

pairs.r: Slower acceleration and a longer ground run
Higher true airspeed needed, and less thrust
Tires sink in, so a longer ground roll

activities.title: Fly it in order
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the steps in order, then tap Check.
steps: Finish the run-up and checklists before taxiing onto the runway
Roll onto the runway without stopping and line up
Add takeoff power smoothly, as fast as the engine accepts it
Use back-elevator pressure to lift the nose-wheel and hold a nose-high attitude
Let the airplane fly itself off, below a safe climb speed
Gently lower the nose with the wheels just clear of the surface
Accelerate in ground effect to at least VX
Climb at VX until obstacles are cleared, then pitch for VY

activities.title: True or false: wind and wake

cards.s: In a crosswind, start the roll with the ailerons neutral and add aileron as you speed up.
cards.why: No. Start the roll with full aileron into the wind and hold it until the ailerons become effective [[24:138|AFH 6-6]]. Then use just enough to keep the wings level [[24:139|AFH 6-7]].

cards.s: In strong, gusty wind, the AFH advises an extra margin of speed before you leave the ground.
cards.why: Yes. At normal speed, a sudden lull could leave you without positive control, or even stall the airplane [[24:137|AFH 6-5]].

cards.s: If the CTAF gives you the wind, you don't need to check the windsock.
cards.why: No. Still check the wind indicators, because there is no assurance the CTAF information is accurate [[1:354|PHAK 14-20]].

cards.s: Near the ground, a larger airplane's wake vortices can drift sideways at about 2 to 3 knots.
cards.why: Yes. Once they sink to within 100 to 200 feet of the ground, they move sideways at 2-3 knots [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]].

cards.s: Taking off behind a departing larger airplane, you should rotate after its rotation point.
cards.why: No. Rotate before its rotation point, then climb above its climb path until you turn clear of its wake [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]] [[24:133|AFH 6-1]].

cards.s: Strong upper winds of more than 25 knots are one clue that low-level wind shear may be present.
cards.why: Yes. Low-level wind shear often comes with fronts, thunderstorms, temperature inversions and upper winds over 25 knots [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]].

final_quiz.q: You taxi toward a muddy grass runway for a soft-field takeoff. Why should you keep the airplane moving as you turn onto the runway?
options: It lets you skip the before-takeoff checklist
Stopping would make P-factor stronger on the roll
Stopping on mud or snow can bog the airplane down
It keeps the airplane in ground effect
final_quiz.why: The AFH says to keep a continuous motion with enough power while lining up, because stopping on a soft surface like mud or snow might bog the airplane down [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].

final_quiz.q: Your POH recommends a flap setting for soft-field takeoffs. When do you set the flaps, and why?
options: Only after reaching VX, to climb more steeply
After lift-off, to help stay in ground effect
Halfway down the runway, once the nose-wheel is up
Before starting the takeoff, to add lift and move weight to the wings sooner
final_quiz.why: Lower the flaps before starting the takeoff, if the manufacturer recommends it, to give extra lift and move the weight to the wings as early as possible [[24:145|AFH 6-13]]. The POH setting wins if it differs from the AFH [[24:133|AFH 6-1]].

final_quiz.q: You are holding the airplane a few feet above the runway, accelerating in ground effect. What will the instruments most likely show?
options: Airspeed and altitude read a bit high, and the VSI shows a climb
Airspeed and altitude read a bit low, and the VSI may show a descent
Every instrument reads exactly right
Airspeed reads high, but the altimeter is exact
final_quiz.why: Ground effect raises the pressure at the static source, so the airspeed indicator and altimeter read slightly low, and the VSI usually shows a descent [[24:142|AFH 6-10]].

final_quiz.q: Your airplane has a 36-foot wingspan. At about what wing height above the runway is the cut in induced drag only 1.4 percent?
options: About 3.6 feet
About 36 feet
About 9 feet
About 72 feet
final_quiz.why: At a height equal to the wingspan, induced drag is cut by only 1.4 percent [[1:108|PHAK 5-11]]. One wingspan here is 36 feet. At 9 feet (1/4 span) the cut is 23.5 percent, and at 3.6 feet (1/10 span) it is 47.6 percent.

final_quiz.q: On a hot day at max gross weight, your airplane lifts off a grass strip early. At full power it floats in ground effect but will not climb. What is the only way to cut the drag?
options: Hold the same attitude and wait for the airplane to climb
Pull the nose higher to climb out of ground effect
Add a little back pressure to hold altitude
Lower the pitch to gain airspeed, even though it costs some altitude
final_quiz.why: Power is already at maximum, so reducing drag is the only option, and that means lowering the pitch and losing some altitude [[24:143|AFH 6-11]]. More back pressure or a higher nose only adds drag. You may be in the region of reversed command, where even full power won't climb [[1:268|PHAK 11-12]].

final_quiz.q: A pilot makes a soft-field takeoff from a strip with open fields and no obstacles past the end. After accelerating in ground effect, which climb speed fits best?
options: VY
Lift-off speed, to keep the climb steep
A speed just below VX
VX all the way to cruise altitude
final_quiz.why: Stay in ground effect until at least VX, then climb. VX is only needed while an obstacle must be cleared [[24:145|AFH 6-13]]. With no obstacle, VY gives the most altitude in the least time [[24:142|AFH 6-10]].

final_quiz.q: Your POH lists VX as 60 knots, and there are trees past the end of the strip. The ACS allows +10/-5 knots in the climb. Which airspeed range meets the standard?
options: 50 to 70 knots
60 to 70 knots
55 to 65 knots
55 to 70 knots
final_quiz.why: 60 + 10 = 70 knots and 60 - 5 = 55 knots (ACS PA.IV.C.S10). Aim for the exact speed anyway: in some airplanes being 5 knots off cuts climb performance a lot [[24:142|AFH 6-10]].

final_quiz.q: In the nose-high soft-field roll at full power, the nose keeps yawing left. Which effects are strongest right now, and what is the fix?
options: Gyroscopic action only; use left aileron
Torque reaction only; steer with the brakes
P-factor and corkscrew slipstream; hold left rudder
P-factor and corkscrew slipstream; hold right rudder
final_quiz.why: The corkscrew slipstream is strongest at high power and low speed [[1:128|PHAK 5-31]], and P-factor is strongest at high angle of attack [[1:129|PHAK 5-32]]. Both yaw the nose left, so use right rudder, not brakes, to stay straight [[24:135|AFH 6-3]].

final_quiz.q: A student lifts off and right away pulls the nose up to climb, still below VX. The airplane sinks back toward the grass even at full power. What went wrong?
options: Climbing out of ground effect before reaching climb speed
Lifting the nose-wheel too early in the roll
Using the flap setting the POH recommends
Holding too much right rudder
final_quiz.why: Leaving ground effect brings more drag, and the airplane tends to settle, even at full power. Stay in ground effect until at least VX [[24:145|AFH 6-13]]. Trying to climb out before reaching climb speed is a listed common error [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].

final_quiz.q: For today's conditions, your POH gives a 900-foot takeoff ground roll and a 600-foot landing ground roll. About how much runway does the AFH say you need to accelerate and then stop?
options: About 1,500 feet
About 900 feet
About 1,200 feet
About 600 feet
final_quiz.why: Adding the POH takeoff and landing ground rolls gives a good estimate of the runway needed to accelerate and then stop [[24:146|AFH 6-14]]. 900 + 600 = 1,500 feet.

final_quiz.q: You reject a takeoff because of an engine fire. Besides power to idle and braking while keeping directional control, what does the AFH say to do?
options: Mixture full rich and fuel pump on
Mixture to idle cutoff and magnetos off
Lift off anyway and circle back to land
Leave the engine running so you can taxi clear
final_quiz.why: If the engine must be shut down for a fire, pull the mixture to idle cutoff and turn the magnetos off. Always follow the manufacturer's emergency procedure too [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].

final_quiz.q: Thunderstorms are near the airport as you start your takeoff roll in a trainer. While you are still on the runway, what may be the only sign of a wind shear encounter?
options: The VSI showing a fast climb
The stall horn sounding right away
Airspeed building more slowly than normal
The engine RPM dropping
final_quiz.why: A headwind that turns into a tailwind cuts airspeed and performance [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]]. On the runway, the only sign may be a slower-than-normal airspeed increase, and gusts can hide it [[28:270|AWH 22-15]].

final_quiz.q: You depart a high-elevation strip on a hot day. Compared with a cool sea-level day, how does your lift-off speed change?
options: Higher indicated airspeed, same true airspeed
Lower indicated airspeed and lower true airspeed
Same indicated airspeed, higher true airspeed
Same true airspeed, lower indicated airspeed
final_quiz.why: At higher density altitude the airplane lifts off at the same indicated airspeed, but the thinner air means a higher true airspeed, and the engine makes less thrust [[1:272|PHAK 11-16]].
